financials.source: Ascension Consolidated Financial Statements Q4 FY2025; Ascension Q4 FY25 news release September 2025; FierceHealthcare; Becker's Hospital Review. Non-operating revenue derived from reported net income of $918M minus operating loss of -$491M. Figures are for consolidated Ascension system (Ascension Health Alliance, EIN 45-3358926).

balanceSheetWealth.investmentPortfolioSource: Ascension Consolidated Financial Statements Q4 FY2025 — long-term investments of $19,449,512 thousand as of June 30, 2025; plus short-term investments of $43,974 thousand
balanceSheetWealth.notes: Substantially all cash and investments are managed by Ascension Investment Management (AIM), a wholly owned subsidiary. More than $1B allocated to alternative investments including private equity and private credit. As of December 31, 2024 (mid-year FY2025), net unrestricted cash and investments were $15B. System had 228 days cash on hand as of June 30, 2025. Ascension manages assets using an endowment-style approach.

bondDebt.largestIssueProceeds: $2.5 billion — issued through authorities in Indiana, Tennessee, and Texas for capital projects and refunding of previously issued tax-exempt bonds; separate $2.1B taxable bond issuance in November 2025 used to defease remaining tax-exempt subordinate bonds
bondDebt.issuerAuthority: Multiple state health facility finance authorities (Indiana, Tennessee, Texas)
bondDebt.source: Ascension Consolidated Financial Statements Q3 FY2025 ($5.6B long-term debt as of March 31, 2025); Fitch Ratings September 2025 (downgrade affected $5.5B in bonds); Bond Buyer; Fitch expects Ascension to issue up to $4.2B in additional debt

otherRelatedEntities: Ascension Investment Management (AIM) — manages substantially all system cash and investments
Ascension Care Management — insurance holdings company
Ascension Rx — pharmacy operations including 340B and specialty pharmacy
Ascension St. Vincent — Indiana market operations and Colts partner
relatedOrganizations.source: Schedule R; Ascension Consolidated Financial Statements; Ascension corporate website; Missouri subsidiary list includes 40+ entities

executiveComp.source: Form 990 FY2023 via ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer and Paddock Post (EIN 45-3358926). Other top executives FY2023: Craig Cordola (EVP/COO) $5,304,408; Eduardo Conrado (Former Board Member) $5,073,352; Elizabeth Foshage (EVP/CFO) $3,981,721; Karen Springer (EVP/CNE) $3,921,283. FY2024 filing shows CEO reportable compensation of $9,963,725 plus $2,317,426 in other compensation ($12,281,151 total). Five-year CEO total (FY2020-2024): approximately $48M.

communityBenefit.source: Ascension community benefit webpage and Ascension Consolidated Financial Statements FY2024. $2.1B in Care of Persons Living in Poverty and Other Community Benefit Programs for FY2024 (ended June 30, 2024). With unpaid costs of Medicare included, total reaches $4.3B. Ascension claims this is four times what it would have paid in taxes as a for-profit company. Percentage calculated against FY2024 total operating revenue of $28.55B.

taxAdvantage.notes: Ascension claims its $2.1B community benefit is four times what it would have paid in taxes as a for-profit company, implying estimated annual tax advantage of approximately $525M. Operates across 15 states and the District of Columbia with significant tax-exempt property holdings. 340B savings in Texas alone were $20.9M in 2023.

layoffs.notes: Ascension confirmed layoffs of employees in Texas; primarily nonclinical support roles; declined to specify number of positions affected

Layoffs and hiring freeze triggered by May 2024 ransomware cyberattack and resulting $1.8B operating loss; number unspecified; New York Times alleged system-wide staffing crisis leading to complaints about possible preventable deaths
layoffs.source: FierceHealthcare; Becker's Hospital Review; New York Times

layoffs.notes: Approximately 500 employees laid off system-wide with reports suggesting total could climb to 1,000; affected locations include Michigan (Ascension St. John), Illinois, Kansas, and Oklahoma
layoffs.source: Crain's Detroit Business; FierceHealthcare; Lime Entrepreneur

facilityClosures.notes: Reduced from approximately 139 hospitals to 90 wholly owned or consolidated hospitals through strategic divestitures as part of post-pandemic operational transformation
facilityClosures.source: Becker's Hospital Review; FierceHealthcare; Becker's ASC Review

facilityClosures.facility: Our Lady of Lourdes Memorial Hospital (Binghamton, NY)

facilityClosures.notes: Joint venture with Henry Ford Health; hospitals folded into partnership

facilityClosures.facility: 9 Illinois/Chicago-area hospitals and 4 senior living facilities
facilityClosures.notes: Sold to Prime Healthcare Services; includes Ascension Holy Family, Ascension Mercy, Ascension Resurrection, Ascension St. Francis, Ascension St. Joseph (Joliet), Ascension St. Joseph (Elgin), Ascension St. Mary (Kankakee), Ascension St. Mary (Chicago), Ascension St. Elizabeth
facilityClosures.source: Religion News Service; Becker's Hospital Review

facilityClosures.notes: Sold to Beacon Health System; Kalamazoo, Allegan, Plainwell, and Dowagiac facilities

keyRiskFactors: Persistent operating losses — $1.8B loss in FY2024, $491M loss in FY2025, $120M loss through FY2026 Q3
Massive hospital divestiture program reducing portfolio from 139 to 90 facilities since 2022
May 2024 ransomware attack exposing 5.4M patient records and contributing to $1.3B in financial impact
Fitch expects up to $4.2B in additional debt issuance, constraining cash-to-debt ratio
Fitch downgraded from AA+ to AA in September 2025 citing inadequate profitability

acquisitions.notes: Acquired for $3.9B; expanded ambulatory surgery center footprint from 58 to 300+ centers across 34 states; FTC required divestiture of 6 facilities to Optum subsidiary SC Affiliates; establishes Ascension as third-largest ASC platform nationally
acquisitions.source: Becker's Hospital Review; FierceHealthcare; Bloomberg; Bond Buyer

lobbying.source: OpenSecrets via JAMA Health Forum study (2026); Ascension spent $2.16M on federal lobbying in 2024, ranking among the top health system lobbying spenders alongside Advocate ($2.42M) and Tenet ($2.2M)

legalIssues.description: Ransomware cyberattack compromised personal and health information of 5.4 million individuals; forced electronic health records offline across 19 states; facilities diverted emergency cases to nearby hospitals; class action lawsuit filed alleging failure to implement essential security measures; plaintiffs allege imminent risk of identity theft, fraudulent charges, delayed care, and protected health information posted to dark web
legalIssues.status: Lawsuit moving forward as of October 2025; one of the largest healthcare data breaches in U.S. history
legalIssues.source: HealthExec; Healthcare Dive; CBS News Detroit; Class Law Group

ratios.investmentsToOperatingIncomeInterpretati: Ratio undefined — Ascension reported a $491M operating loss in FY2025. However, the system holds $19.4B in long-term investments (39.6x the magnitude of the operating loss), indicating massive accumulated wealth persisting through sustained operating losses.
ratios.bondDebtToCommunityBenefitInterpretation: Ascension carries $2.67 in tax-exempt bond debt for every $1 it claims in community benefit ($5.6B debt vs $2.1B community benefit)
ratios.charityCareVsStateInterpretation: State average not verified; charity care component of Ascension's $2.1B total community benefit not separately available from search results

accusation: Ascension holds $19.4 billion in long-term investments atop $39.9 billion in total assets while posting a $491 million operating loss in FY2025, carrying $5.6 billion in tax-exempt bond debt, paying its CEO $9.1 million, divesting nearly 50 hospitals, and cutting hundreds of jobs — yet claims just $2.1 billion in community benefit on $25.3 billion in revenue.
